meta.title: Who really said "Science and everyday life cannot and should not be separated"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Yes — Rosalind Franklin wrote it, aged 19, in a 1940 letter to her father defending science against his complaint that she was one-sided.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'Science and everyday life cannot and should not be separated'?
meta.ogDescription: Genuinely Rosalind Franklin — from her 1940 letter to her father, quoted in Brenda Maddox's biography 'The Dark Lady of DNA' (pp. 60–61).

answer.label: Written by
answer.sourceLine: From a letter the 19-year-old Franklin wrote to her father, Ellis Franklin, in the summer of 1940, defending science against his charge that she had a “one-sided” outlook. The line is quoted from the original letter in Brenda Maddox’s 2002 biography “Rosalind Franklin: The Dark Lady of DNA.”

source.heading: Where it comes from

docMeta.dd: Summer 1940, in a letter to her father Ellis Franklin
Rosalind Franklin: The Dark Lady of DNA

source.excerpt: But you look at science (or at least talk of it) as some sort of demoralising invention of man, something apart from real life, and which must be cautiously guarded and kept separate from everyday existence. But science and everyday life cannot and should not be separated. Science, for me, gives a partial explanation of life.
trail: Traced in detail by Quote Investigator ↗, which locates the line in Brenda Maddox’s biography and dates the letter to Franklin’s Cambridge years (1938–1941).
Humanists UK’s Humanist Heritage ↗ reproduces the same 1940 letter, treating it as a statement of Franklin’s humanist outlook on science and faith.
The U.S. National Library of Medicine ↗ documents Franklin’s life and work on DNA, coal, and virus structure, confirming the biographical frame.
source.cutTag: ↑ the popular one-liner drops the leading “But” and the rebuttal it answers
source.excerptNote: The famous sentence is Franklin’s direct reply to her father, who had accused her of a “completely one-sided” outlook. In the same letter she set out an essentially humanist creed — “all that is necessary for faith is the belief that by doing our best we shall come nearer to success” — and added, “Science, for me, gives a partial explanation of life.”

author.name: Rosalind Franklin
author.heading: About Rosalind Franklin
author.bio: Rosalind Franklin (1920–1958) was a British chemist and X-ray crystallographer whose diffraction images of DNA — notably “Photograph 51” — were pivotal to Watson and Crick’s model of the double helix, and who also did foundational work on the structure of coal and of viruses. She wrote this line at nineteen, while a student at Newnham College, Cambridge, in reply to her father’s worry that science had made her one-sided. She died of ovarian cancer at just 37, before the Nobel that honoured the DNA work could recognise her contribution.

context.heading: Why it mattered
lead: Franklin was nineteen and studying at Cambridge when her father, Ellis, wrote to complain that science had given her a “completely one-sided” outlook and that she treated it almost as a religion. This sentence is her rebuttal: science is not a walled-off discipline to be “kept separate from everyday existence,” but part of the fabric of a whole life.

In the same letter she sketched a secular, humanist faith — the conviction that by doing our best we improve the lot of humankind — making the line as much about how to live as about how to do research.
detailsBody: Franklin identified as culturally Jewish but was not religious; the 1940 letter is one of the clearest surviving statements of her worldview, which is why humanist organisations and biographers alike return to it. The single sentence has since taken on a life of its own on posters and quote sites, usually stripped of the “But” and of the father-daughter argument that gave it its point.
